img_c8cee9c9c1dee867.title: Clearing land for Beaumont's new fire station, 650 Maple Ave. — Record-Gazette, March 21, 1969
img_c8cee9c9c1dee867.description: A photographed newspaper page — headline 'Beaumont's New Fire Station,' photo caption 'Clearing Fire Station Land' — showing bulldozers grading the fire-station site at 650 Maple Ave., just north of Sixth St., while two men look on. The accompanying article, legible in the image, reports that official groundbreaking ceremonies took place the morning of Nov. 27, 1968, and that completion of the 3,600-square-foot central station would let the police department under Chief Jack Richardson expand into the old fire quarters at City Hall. It also records Fire Chief Mickey Wright's plan for a second station south of the freeway and Southern Pacific tracks, and that citizen Fred Hirsch contracted to build the $30,000 facility, to be repaid by the city over a period of years, with L.R. Daniel offering property at B St. and Minnesota Ave. for the southside station. A sibling scan in the BLD folder is filenamed '3-21-69 Record-Gazette,' dating the page to the March 21, 1969 issue. The completed station — today's Fire Station 66 — is recorded by the Beaumont Library District at 628 Maple Ave., and photographs of it in 1971 are on Calisphere.

img_b2764c9151e44824.title: Beaumont Land and Water Company office, Beaumont, c. 1907-1915
img_b2764c9151e44824.original_title: Beaumont Land And Water Company From Beaumont Library District
img_b2764c9151e44824.description: A mounted print, hand-captioned 'Office at Beaumont' on the mat, showing the Beaumont Land and Water Company's small Mission Revival office: tiled parapet roof with scrolled end caps, three arched bays, a fresh concrete sidewalk, and an unpaved street. The main signboard reads 'Beaumont Land and Water Co.'; the left window carries arched lettering reading '[S]an Gorgonio / Water Co.' and the right window 'Land … Water Co.' The company purchased the Beaumont townsite and several thousand adjoining acres and promoted them relentlessly — 453 Chronicling America hits, overwhelmingly the Los Angeles Herald, run from Oct. 6, 1907 through 1910, recording biweekly excursions, day-and-night well drilling (1908), the Cherry Valley subdivision (1908), the La Mesa Miravilla tract (1909), and enlarged Los Angeles headquarters at 616 South Broadway (1909). That campaign drove the boom that carried Beaumont to incorporation on Nov. 18, 1912. The building's style and new-built appearance place the photograph within the company's active years, c. 1907-1915 — the company is not documented before 1907, so the previous 1890-1905 range cannot stand.
corrections: Date corrected from c. 1890-1905 to c. 1907-1915: the company is not documented before October 1907, and a tiled-parapet Mission Revival office is anachronistic for the 1890s.
Window lettering ('[S]an Gorgonio / Water Co.' left, 'Land … Water Co.' right) read from enlarged crops of the print and added to the record.
Historical context added: the company's townsite purchase and 1907-1910 sales campaign (LA Herald via Chronicling America) preceding Beaumont's 1912 incorporation.

That anchors this photograph at 1955, two years before Bogart's death; he is buried in Stewart Sunnyslope Cemetery, Beaumont.

img_1ace86d145209734.title: Chancel of the Beaumont Presbyterian 'Rock Church,' 702 Euclid Ave. — modern interior view
img_1ace86d145209734.description: A modern color photograph of the chancel of the Beaumont Presbyterian 'Rock Church' at 702 Euclid Ave. (northeast corner of 7th and Euclid): a brass Celtic-style cross spotlit against the arched cobblestone apse, a carved communion table with a partially legible Gothic inscription, paired candlesticks, an open Bible, U.S. and Christian flags, and large arrangements of red roses and white lilies. The photograph itself is recent: consumer digital color with modern lighting and cellophane-wrapped florals, no earlier than the 2000s and no later than the assembly of the BLD digital folder (sibling files carry received dates of 2020-2023). The previous 1934-2025 date range described the building, not the photograph.

img_c6fa941a29b0f0cd.description: Hand-colored postcard captioned 'Hotel Edinburgh, Beaumont, California,' showing the twin-towered Queen Anne boom hotel behind mature gardens and palms. It stood at Fifth Street and Beaumont Avenue, roughly where I-10 now crosses Beaumont Avenue. Because the card bears the Edinburgh name, the view and publication belong to the c. 1907-1909 window. The file is a small web scan bearing an ePodunk.com watermark at lower right, not a library original.

img_df9bd9231a83651c.title: Reznor Perry Stewart (1845-1933), Beaumont pioneer rancher — halftone portrait
img_df9bd9231a83651c.description: A screened halftone portrait, reproduced from an unidentified printed publication, of Reznor Perry Stewart (3 Nov 1845 - 12 Nov 1933), seated in three-quarter view with a full white beard, dark suit, and watch chain. Stewart was one of Beaumont's founding ranchers: Holmes' 1912 county history records that 'R. P. Stewart and Dan Scott commenced raising grain' in 1884 and that Stewart was still living on his grain and hay ranch in 1912, and BLD's Calisphere Beaumont Bank item adds that he was one of the founders of the Beaumont Bank (built 1911) and its president for several years. The family name survives in Stewart Ranch and in Stewart Sunnyslope Cemetery, Beaumont, where he is buried with his daughter Laura May (1884-1974) and son Reznor P. Jr. (1890-1907). His apparent age — sixties to seventies — against the 1845 birth date places the sitting around 1905-1920. This is print 'c' of three copies of the same portrait in the BLD folder; the publication it came from has not been identified, and the Google-scanned volume of the 1912 county history contains no Stewart portrait or biography.

img_7dad1702b8b44459.title: Stewart Sunny Slope Cemetery Entrance Gate Dedication, Memorial Day 1962
img_7dad1702b8b44459.description: Black-and-white 8x10 print, photographed lying on a black album page and hand-dated 'May 30, 1962' below the image. Six older adults pose at the new wrought-iron entrance arch reading 'STEWART / SUNNY SLOPE CEMETE[RY]'; two men wear American Legion-style overseas caps, a man at center holds his hat, and the man at right gestures toward a bronze plaque set into the rock-faced gate pillar reading (partially legible) 'THIS GATEWAY ... [REZNOR P.] STEWART FAMILY.' The Record-Gazette confirms that on Memorial Day, May 30, 1962, the Beaumont Cemetery District dedicated this new entrance gate, made in the name of the Reznor P. Stewart family — 'for years major donors of land' to the cemetery — represented by Laura Stewart and Clara Stewart; the cemetery was renamed Stewart Sunny Slope Cemetery in the family's honor the same year. The two elderly women in the group are therefore very likely Laura May and Clara Stewart, daughters of ranch founder Reznor P. Stewart. Sunny Slope cemetery burials are documented from at least 1915 (Art Stewart's interment). This Beaumont cemetery is distinct from Banning's similarly named Sunnyslope Cemetery (now San Gorgonio Memorial Park).

img_7b302ec1a5a6c157.title: Reznor P. Stewart, Founder of the Stewart Ranch, Late-Life Snapshot, c. 1910-1933
img_7b302ec1a5a6c157.description: An elderly man with a full white beard, wearing a broad-brimmed hat and a vest over a work shirt, stands behind a wire fence in front of a ranch house, with garden flowers at lower right — a small amateur snapshot, unannotated and low-resolution in this copy. He is Reznor P. Stewart (c. 1845-1933), who homesteaded at Beaumont in 1883 and, buying additional Southern Pacific railroad land, built the Stewart Ranch to more than 2,200 acres of grain and hay; a 1974 obituary of his daughter calls him 'the first grain farmer in the area,' and he was a founder and long-time president of the Beaumont Bank (built 1911 as the Funk Building). He died in November 1933 at age 88 — a San Bernardino Sun item of 13 Nov 1933 describes 'Reznor P. Stewart, 88 years old and prominent in affairs...', and Notices to Creditors for his estate (No. 6530, with Laura M. Stewart as special administrator) ran in the Beaumont Daily Gazette from January 1934. His evident old age places the snapshot in roughly his last two decades, not the catalog's former 1900-1915 range. In 1962 Beaumont's cemetery was renamed Stewart Sunny Slope Cemetery in his family's honor.
corrections: Date range changed from c. 1900-1915 to c. 1910-1933: he died November 1933 aged 88, and the sitter's evident old age plus the amateur-snapshot format point to his later years.
Added life dates (c. 1845 - Nov 1933) from his death notice and estate probate notices.

img_cd302d98752b29e0.title: Second Bank of Beaumont Entrance, Fifth Street and California Avenue, c. 1923-1940
img_cd302d98752b29e0.original_title: Second Bank Of Beaumont From Beaumont Library District
img_cd302d98752b29e0.description: Warm-toned street-level view of the arched entrance bay of the second Bank of Beaumont, with a carved archivolt and pediment ornament over the recessed double door, a tall multi-pane window at right, and a parapet cartouche above; a large eucalyptus leans over the sidewalk at left, where two children in coats walk away past distant storefronts. The building was erected in 1923 by Fred Hirsch, a large Beaumont real-estate holder, replacing the town's outgrown first bank; its surviving parapet is incised 'BANK OF BEAUMONT — FOUNDED 1909, ERECTED 1923,' and the building still stands at Fifth Street and California Avenue. The 1923 construction gives the firm start of the date range; the empty street, the children's dress, and the bank's continued operation (its sign came down only in 1950, 'ending a chapter' per the Daily Gazette) are consistent with the collection's c. 1923-1940 estimate. Calisphere's Banning Library District slide of the same building is dated 'circa 1920,' which is impossible for a 1923 building, and its BLD/Calisphere descriptions inconsistently place it at 'Fifth and Egan' — the facade inscription and the surviving building support Fifth and California.

img_5430b97f619e1088.title: Presbyterian Church postcard, northeast corner of 7th and Euclid Streets
img_5430b97f619e1088.original_title: Community Church (Beaumont Presbyterian Church) — real-photo postcard
img_5430b97f619e1088.description: Real-photo postcard view of Beaumont's Presbyterian 'Rock Church' at the northeast corner of 7th and Euclid Streets, hand-captioned 'COMMUNITY CHURCH' in white at upper left; an announcement board and a white curb post stand at the corner entrance beneath shade trees. The congregation is the oldest in Beaumont, dating to April 17, 1885, and in 1925 was known as the Federated Church of Beaumont, its membership drawn from 14 denominations. The stone sanctuary shown here was completed May 20, 1934 at a cost of $11,009, built by hand from rocks that members and friends gathered from Whitewater. Its rock construction, portals, and unique design make it a Beaumont city landmark; the social hall dates to the same era.
corrections: Title changed from the local working title to Calisphere's 'Presbyterian Church postcard, northeast corner of 7th and Euclid Streets' — Calisphere confirms the postcard's 'Community Church' hand caption denotes the Beaumont Presbyterian Rock Church, and pins the corner as 7th and Euclid.

Attribution changed from 'Unknown (postcard photographer/publisher unidentified)' to Beaumont Library District Local History Collection, via Calisphere (CBEA_163), on the strength of the confirmed visual match; the postcard photographer/publisher itself remains unidentified.

Rights determined: Copyrighted — the Calisphere rights statement names the Beaumont Chamber of Commerce (previously unassessed). Rule 2 pre-1931 public-domain override considered and rejected because the sanctuary was not completed until May 20, 1934.

Date range floor corroborated: the May 20, 1934 sanctuary completion in the Calisphere description supports the record's existing 1934-1960 range; Calisphere's date field is empty, so no date override is made.

Four more wells would follow, along with reservoirs to store the water. The print carries a white damage spot at top center that also appears in the Calisphere copy, confirming it is the same physical print.

img_3f09693198e8de04.title: The Summit House, Beaumont
img_3f09693198e8de04.description: A large crowd of men and women in dark late-Victorian dress poses in front of a two-story wood-frame hotel, with a painted 'SUMMIT HOUSE' sign mounted across the vine-covered porch and a 'BEAUMONT LAND AND WATER COMPANY' inscription running along the top of the print; the upper-left corner of the print is torn away diagonally. The Summit House was Beaumont's first hotel, established in 1884 by Frank Mindler; it began as the Beatty House and was later renovated and renamed. It catered to large groups needing lodging on special occasions — such as Smoot and Eyer's prospective land buyers — and burned down in 1925. img_43eb34083eb2296d.title: Edinburgh Hotel Real Estate Banquet, near 5th and Beaumont Ave
img_43eb34083eb2296d.description: A rare interior view of a real estate banquet at the Edinburgh Hotel, preserved as a rounded-corner print on a black album page bearing the typed label "EDINBURGH HOTEL / REAL ESTATE BANQUET." Families in Edwardian dress — including several children and a baby in a bonnet — sit at round, white-clothed tables beneath interior columns and an early chandelier, most faces turned toward the camera, with a second set table visible at right. Per the Calisphere description, John D. Revis is turned toward J. Drew Funk, the young man at the center of the photo. The three-story Victorian building opened in 1887 as the Beaumont Hotel, later closed, reopened in 1907 as the Hotel Edinburgh, and came to a fiery end in August 1909; it stood on Beaumont Avenue where the El Rancho Restaurant and Best Western Rancho Motel were later located.

img_e8c5738ad26c5ffc.title: Laura Mae Stewart, First Cherry Festival Queen, Riding in a Studebaker Six at the 2nd Cherry Festival
img_e8c5738ad26c5ffc.description: A decorated Studebaker Six touring car photographed beneath a pepper tree, canopied with draped fabric and ribbons for the 2nd Cherry Festival parade; a placard at the running board is lettered "BEAUMONT GARAGE AND MACHINE CO. / STUDEBAKER SIX." and a "Studebaker" script pennant hangs at the rear, with a ribbon streaming forward to a bow at the radiator. Queen Laura Mae Stewart — the festival's first queen — is seated in the center rear seat, with Princesses Lois Behu on her right and Clara Dietrich on her left; Lawrence Rulier, in uniform up front, is the queen's escort, and E. O. Jones is the driver. Per Calisphere, the first Cherry Festival began in 1913 with great success, and the following year Laura Mae Stewart became its first queen; the Studebaker was brought out from Los Angeles to carry the queen in the parade. A second open car and a house are visible in the background.

img_477fd73b5434521f.description: Sepia print of the entrance to John J. McCoy's lumberyard in Beaumont: a picket fence and gate shaded by large pepper trees, with a long painted sign reading "LUMBER-YARD" over a smaller, partly legible line of lettering, a dirt road and a culvert drain in the foreground, and yard buildings and stacked lumber behind the fence.
